prompt: One wildcat with pos 0.3, a success-case NPV of 300 and a fail cost of 50. A normal approximation puts its P90 at -150.5560. What is wrong with that figure?
options: Nothing is wrong with it: a low case set beneath the worst outcome is a conservative margin, and the simulation has simply removed that margin.
It is the high case with its sign reversed, because the normal curve ranks outcomes under the opposite percentile convention to the one the engine uses.
It sits beneath -50.0000, the worst outcome the well can produce, so it describes a loss this project can never book.
It is right for the success case alone, since the normal curve is fitted to the success spread and leaves the failure lump out of the sum.
explanation: The normal P90 is emv minus 1.2816 x stdDev on a bell the well does not have: it fails with chance 0.700000 and then loses exactly 50.0000, which is the engine's P90, -50.0000.

prompt: A reviewer proposes keeping the normal approximation and adding a fixed safety margin to its P(loss). The identical wildcat cases read 0.276275 against an exact 0.343000 for three wells and 0.200464 against 0.117649 for six. Why does the margin fail?
options: The error changes sign as wells are added, understated with three and overstated with six, so no single margin leans the right way.
A fixed margin would have to be reset for every seed, since the approximation is redrawn on each run.
The margin would move P(loss) and leave P90 untouched, because the approximation read the two figures off two different fitted curves.
The approximation is already conservative on every published case, so a margin double counts risk.
explanation: An error that flips sign cannot be corrected by leaning one way: with eight wells it understates again, 0.166046 against an exact 0.255298.

prompt: On which published cases does the normal approximation give the exact P(loss)?
options: The large identical wildcat cases, where eight wells are enough outcomes for the lumps to converge on a normal curve and the approximation settles.
The comonotone cases, where every project fails together, so the portfolio behaves as one project and a single fitted curve describes it exactly.
The three mixed wildcats, where the different fail costs spread the lumps apart and smooth the sum into the shape of a normal distribution.
The pos1-normal cases, projects that always succeed with a normal spread, where the portfolio value really is a bell.
explanation: normalPairIndependent reads 0.001571 both ways and normalThreeCorrelated 0.231959, while comonotoneIdentical3 reads 0.365832 against 0.700000 and identical8 0.166046 against 0.255298.

prompt: In a simulated iteration where OK-3 fails, what does the engine book for it?
options: Its npv_p90 of 210.0000, the low percentile of its entered range, which is the value a well lands on when its success driver misses.
Minus 85.0000 exactly, in every failing iteration, since the success spread scales a success and a failure is a single number.
Minus 85.0000 plus its success spread of 191.1747 times z2, because both of its drivers are drawn in every iteration and both are applied.
A normal draw around minus 85.0000 scaled by its mixture sd of 238.6507, which folds in the failure lump.
explanation: OK-3 fails with chance 0.750000 and books 85.0000 of loss each time, which is why its risked EMV is 0.250000 x 420.0000 - 0.750000 x 85.0000 = 41.2500 and why small portfolios have spikes.

prompt: mixtureWithSpread pairs a risked project with a sure one. A normal approximation puts its P90 at -12.4175; the simulation reads 1.7148. What would a reader of the normal figure get wrong?
options: Nothing of substance, since both figures sit close to zero and the gap between them is inside one standard error of the simulated count.
The sign of the high case, because under the exceedance convention the normal P90 is the figure a committee would quote as the upside.
That the low case loses money, when nine simulated outcomes in ten are gains.
The worst case, because a P90 of -12.4175 is the floor of the portfolio and the simulation shows the floor is really a small gain.
explanation: Under the exceedance convention P90 is the 10th percentile of simulated portfolio NPV, and at 1.7148 it is a gain; the bell fitted to emv and stdDev put it at a loss of 12.4175.

prompt: OK-3's npv_p10 of 700.0000 sits further above its npv_p50 of 420.0000 than its npv_p90 of 210.0000 sits below it. What does the simulation keep of that shape?
options: The skew as well, since a success above the median is scaled by the upper half of the range and one below it by the narrower lower half.
Nothing of the percentiles at all, because a project with pos 0.250000 is drawn from its mixture sd of 238.6507 on every iteration.
The upper half of the range only, since a success is never drawn below its npv_p50 of 420.0000 and a failure books the downside instead.
Only the width, as a success spread of 191.1747 drawn symmetrically around 420.0000, so the skew is discarded.
explanation: The success spread is (700.0000 - 210.0000) / 2.5631 = 191.1747 and z2 is a symmetric normal, so a wide spread can occasionally put a success below zero.

prompt: Two runs at the default seed differ only in one project's pos. Why is the gap between their results readable as the effect of that change?
options: The draw order never depends on the inputs, so every project receives the same normals in both runs and only the change moves the result.
The engine reseeds each project from its id, so a project whose pos is untouched redraws exactly what it drew before, while the edited one draws afresh.
A project with a different pos skips its unused e1 draw, and skipping one normal shifts the stream by a known amount that the engine corrects for.
The seed advances by one for each run, so two runs always differ by a single step of sampling noise and the rest of the gap is the edit.
explanation: Each iteration draws F1, F2, then e1 and e2 per project in array order from mulberry32(20260829), and every normal is drawn whether or not it is used.

prompt: An analyst lists the 450.0000 set's projects in a different order and P(loss) moves off 0.123600, with the seed and iterations unchanged. Why?
options: The optimizer breaks ties by entry order, so the reordered list funds a different set at 450.0000 and the risk summary is simulated for that set.
F1 and F2 are drawn after the last project, so moving a project changes which shared draws it hears.
The e1 and e2 normals are dealt to projects in array order, so a new order hands each project different draws and the figure moves by sampling noise.
The grid charges cells in entry order, so the reordered set weighs differently and its capex is simulated at a new total.
explanation: The set is still OK-1 + OK-3 + OK-4 and the seed still 20260829; anyone reproducing a figure needs the seed, the iteration count and the project order.

prompt: A team tries seeds until P(loss) for OKONO's 450.0000 set prints 0.119100, which seed 3 gives, and reports that figure. The default seed reads 0.123600 with a standard error of 0.003291. What is the problem with the report?
options: There is none, because every seed is exactly reproducible and any reproducible figure is as true as the default one.
0.119100 is below the exact P(loss) of the set, which the engine prints as 0.123600 whenever it runs at its default seed.
0.119100 is a 1000 iteration figure, since the engine drops to 1000 iterations whenever a seed other than the default is given.
It picks the draw that flatters the set and reduces no risk; an honest report names the seed and iterations beside the figure.
explanation: At 10000 iterations seeds 1 to 3 give 0.119100 to 0.128500; each is reproducible and none is the answer, and a difference smaller than the standard error is noise.

prompt: A user runs the risk summary with a seed that is not a whole number and an iteration count of 0. What runs?
options: Seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations, the defaults, taken silently in place of what was typed.
Nothing: the input is refused with an error, as a negative capex is.
The seed rounded to a whole number and one iteration, the smallest sample it takes.
The closed-form emv and stdDev only, with P(loss), P90 and P10 returned as null because no simulation could be drawn.
explanation: A seed that is not a whole number falls back to 20260829 and an iteration count below 1 falls back to 10000, so the figures are the default run whatever the label says.

prompt: The engine counts P(loss) 0.696100 for the single wildcat against an exact 0.700000, with a standard error of 0.004583. Is the engine wrong?
options: Yes, because a reproducible seeded run ought to land on the exact P(loss).
Yes, because the strict test drops iterations that net exactly zero, which biases the count below the exact loss chance.
No, it sits 0.8510 standard errors from the exact figure, where a count from 10000 iterations should land.
No, because the engine rounds P(loss) to the nearest standard error before printing it.
explanation: probLoss is a proportion with standard error sqrt(p(1 - p) / n); the largest z on the published cases is 1.4289, and a normal approximation's 0.365832 sits dozens of standard errors away.

prompt: identical6 loses with chance 0.117649 and OKONO's 450.0000 set with 0.123600. What does the pair show?
options: identical6 is the safer portfolio, since its loss chance is lower and six wells spread the risk.
P(loss) counts how often and never how much: every identical6 loss is -300.0000, while the 450.0000 set's low case is -18.3574.
The two carry the same downside, because equal loss chances over 10000 iterations imply equal average losses when those losses happen.
The 450.0000 figure is the weaker one, because a set whose successes carry a spread cannot be counted and is approximated instead.
explanation: identical6 loses only when all six wells fail at 50.0000 each; two portfolios with nearly the same P(loss) can hold very different downsides, so the figure is read beside the low case.

prompt: The 600.0000 set reads P(loss) 0.001800 and the 450.0000 set 0.123600. A committee concludes the optimizer picked a safer set at 600.0000. What is wrong?
options: The optimizer maximises risked EMV under the limit and never reads P(loss), so the lower figure is a by-product of a different budget's set.
Nothing, since the engine deducts each candidate set's simulated loss chance from its EMV before solving, so safety is part of every choice it makes.
The two figures come from different seeds, since each limit is simulated on a seed of its own and the comparison mixes two samples.
The 600.0000 set looks safer only because it holds more projects, and the optimizer is written to prefer the larger set whenever two sets tie.
explanation: Both sets were simulated at seed 20260829 and 10000 iterations; a committee that wants less loss chance has to state that as its own constraint and test sets by hand.

prompt: The engine prints P(loss) 0.001800 for OKONO's 600.0000 set, to six decimals. What should a reader add before relying on it?
options: Nothing, because six decimals at 10000 iterations resolve a loss probability to one part in a million and leave no room for error.
The exact P(loss) the risk summary prints beside every OKONO set, which is the figure the simulated count is there to confirm.
The normal approximation's 0.002555, which is the more precise figure for a small probability because it needs no count.
Its standard error, worked by hand as sqrt(p(1 - p) / n), because the engine prints none and a small count is the least precise relative to its size.
explanation: Few iterations fall below zero at 0.001800, so the count rests on a handful of draws; the engine reports no exact figure for OKONO and no standard error beside any P(loss).

prompt: identical8 is eight wildcats, each pos 0.3, 300 on success and a fail cost of 50. The engine's P90 is -50.0000. What outcome is that?
options: The worst case, since P90 under the exceedance convention is the floor beneath which no simulated outcome of the portfolio falls.
The 10th percentile: one success at 300 and seven failures at 50 each, a low case the portfolio reaches but not its worst, which is all eight failing.
A single well's failure, because the engine reports the P90 of the largest funded project in place of a percentile of the whole portfolio.
The high case of the portfolio, the value exceeded by only one outcome in ten, which the exceedance convention labels P90.
explanation: P90 is the low case, the 10th percentile of simulated portfolio NPV. The engine reports no minimum, so the worst outcome of a risked set is written by hand, here eight failures at 50.0000 each.
